She writes of marriage and manners with a gentle sting. The novel charms readers who like quiet comedy of society.
midnight:
Octavus Roy Cohen published this detective novel in 1921. Cohen was already known for The Crimson Alibi and Gray Dusk. The story begins out of a storm, with a suit-case that must be opened. A chapter heading gives the detective's rule: find the woman.

The investigator Carroll interviews visitors, a valet, and several women tied to the case. Hazel Gresham, Evelyn Rogers, and Roland Warren all enter the inquiry. Later chapters return to the suit-case, a woman in a taxi, and a suspect with no alibi. Cohen builds a period mystery of clues, accusations, and loose ends.
nasa-tm-19650003087-pressure-measurement:
Earl R Keener, at the High-Speed Flight Station at Edwards in California, reported flight pressure readings for a delta wing in October 1959. The wing was conically cambered, meaning its surface was curved in a cone-like way. The aircraft was the F-102A, and speeds were transonic, near the speed of sound.

Keener presents pressures measured in real flight, not in a tunnel. Flight data check whether tunnel results hold on a real aircraft. For a cambered delta wing, those readings matter for lift and control. The report preserves that measured record.
nasa-tm-19670026211-preliminary-results-:
C. Catoe, W. Nordberg, P. Thaddeus, and G. Ling, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this report in August 1967. It gives early results from aircraft flight tests of an electrically scanning microwave radiometer. The instrument was designed for a meteorological satellite, and scanning its beam electronically, with no moving antenna, promised a sturdier sensor.

Flown on NASA's Convair 990 aircraft, the radiometer proved that satellite radiation measurements could extend from the infrared into much longer microwave wavelengths. Its phased-array antenna swept a narrow beam sideways across the flight path, building two-dimensional maps of Earth's brightness temperature. Flights crossed Arctic Ocean ice, Alaskan tundra and snow, southwestern deserts, midwestern farmland, Yucatan forests, and storms over land and water. Preliminary displays showed the instrument performing as expected. Land-water and ice contrasts mapped clearly under all cloud conditions, and ocean storm activity could be identified positively.
nasa-tm-19670028348-synthesis-of-ultrahi:
Li-Chen Hsu, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, presented this paper at a polymers meeting in Cleveland, Ohio, in April 1967. It covers the making of poly(ethylene terephthalate), the plastic called PET, with very long molecule chains. Such ultrahigh molecular weight material was wanted to test how chain length affects PET's behavior at cryogenic temperatures, where aerospace uses were in view.

Hsu prepared PET with an average molecular weight on the order of one hundred twenty thousand, starting from commercial grade material. The reaction ran in the solid state inside a gas chromatograph apparatus, an unusual piece of equipment for polymer synthesis. Parameters studied included the catalyst, particle size, and the molecular weight of the starting material. Reaction temperature and time mattered, as did the nature and flow rate of the carrier gas sweeping through the apparatus.
nasa-tm-19690018398-sounding-rocket-para:
Brian C. Pierman, of Goddard Space Flight Center's Flight Program Office, prepared this March 1969 report, X-326-69-162, on sounding rocket parameters versus flight reliability. He compares two physical parameters, flight weight and telemetry channel count, against flight failure rates. The purpose is practical: choosing which environmental tests sounding rocket payloads should have to pass before flying.

A clear correlation is established between greater weight and decreased flight success, Pierman reports. No correlation is established between telemetry channels and flight success. Charts track failure percentages for Apache and Aerobee rockets across moving weight brackets. The finding gives test planners a simple rule: heavier payloads deserve the closer look, while channel count alone signals nothing.
now-or-never-or-the-adventures-of-bobby-:
Oliver Optic wrote Now or Never, or the Adventures of Bobby Bright, as a story for young folks. William T. Adams, his real name, entered it in Massachusetts in 1856. This new edition came from the Mershon Company in New York, under an 1884 copyright. The book is dedicated to his nephew, Charles Henry Pope.

A front picture shows Bobby declaring he is big enough to protect his mother, and will do it. That line, from page forty-two, sets the hero's stamp. Optic wrote boys who work, save, and stand up at home. Young America of his day read such tales for both fun and example. Bobby's adventures test a poor boy's grit.
pictures-in-colour-of-the-isle-of-wight:
Pictures in Colour of the Isle of Wight, from Jarrold and Sons, contains fifty coloured pictures with descriptive notes. The foreword calls the island a resort of varied attractions: cliffs and bays for coast scenery, old mills and cottages for lovers of sylvan beauty. The rugged Landslip and Undercliff furnish romantic interest. Geologists, it adds, can study many formations within short distances, and botanists find wild flowers and ferns in variety.

The pictures reproduce actual photographs, true to nature. The first note treats Steephill Castle near Ventnor. The book ends by calling the island the Garden of England, and inviting readers to come and see.
raabe-german-moonlight:
Moonlight falls on small-town Germany in Wilhelm Raabe's novella German Moonlight, presented here in English. Ordinary people carry inner lives far richer than their quiet streets suggest. Raabe, often called the German Dickens, specialized in exactly that discovery, and this tale shows his method at its gentlest.

Warm humor and quiet melancholy share the telling, as old memories stir under the moon's calm light. Nothing sensational happens; everything human does. Raabe trusted readers to find depth without being shouted at. The novella makes a gentle, moonlit entry into his large and rewarding body of work. Those who enjoy it will find a whole shelf of his fiction waiting in both languages.
recent-developments-in-european-thought:
F. S. Marvin arranged and edited this set of essays on fresh turns in European thought, issued by Oxford University Press in 1920. The book belongs to the Unity Series, and Marvin, author of The Living Past, wrote its opening general survey himself. A line from Shelley's Prometheus Unbound stands as the book's motto.

Four scholars then take up one field each. Professor A. E. Taylor of St. Andrews writes on philosophy, and Dr. F. B. Jevons of Durham on religion. Professor C. H. Herford of Manchester treats poetry, and G. P. Gooch treats history. Each essay maps what had lately changed in its field for general readers.
ships-that-pass-in-the-night:
A two-part novel unfolds in these chapters, with no author named on the pages at hand. Part One brings a newcomer to a health resort world, where Mrs. Reffold learns her lesson and a figure called the Disagreeable Man draws all eyes. Bernardine stands at the tale's warm center.

Chapters trace a betrothal, a love letter, and ships that speak each other in passing. Part Two opens with the dusting of books. Invalids, travelers, and caretakers cross paths briefly and part changed. The title's image of brief meetings governs a tale of kindness between strangers who may never meet again.
swimming-scientifically-taught:
Prof. Frank Eugen Dalton, instructor in scientific swimming at the Dalton Swimming School and originator of the Dalton Method, wrote Swimming Scientifically Taught as a practical manual for young and old. A portrait of Dalton fronts the title page, and a chapter on advanced strokes by Louis C. Dalton of the same school completes the book.

The Daltons teach swimming as a science of strokes, breathing, and body position rather than a knack picked up by splashing. Their method aimed at learners who feared the water as much as at swimmers chasing form and speed. Manuals of this kind, sold with a named system and a family school behind it, belonged to the age when physical culture experts promised methodical mastery of every bodily art.
the-boy-knight: G. A. Henty wrote The Boy Knight: A Tale of the Crusades, dated 1882. Henty had also written The Young Buglers, Through the Fray, The Cornet of Horse, and The Young Colonists. The chapter list starts with The Outlaws and A Rescue. The Capture of Wortham Hold comes third. Then a chapter named for the Crusades leads into making ready, the lists, revenge, and the attack. The list stops at the ninth chapter, whose head is not shown. No page of the tale itself is given here.
the-celtic-twilight:
W. B. Yeats opens this Irish book with a short poem on time and decay, then a verse piece called The Hosting of the Sidhe. In that poem the fairy host rides from Knocknarea, with Caolte tossing his burning hair and Niamh calling mortals away. The host warns that it comes between any watcher and both the deed of his hand and the hope of his heart.

A prose opening, headed This Book, states Yeats's method plainly. He wished, like every artist, to build a small world from the fine and telling things of a flawed world. He aimed to show something of the face of Ireland to his own people. So he wrote down, with care and candor, much that he had heard and seen, adding little that he had merely made up.
the-child-under-eight: E. R. Murray, Vice-Principal of Maria Grey Training College, and Henrietta Brown Smith, a lecturer at Goldsmiths' College, wrote this study of young children in the Modern Educator's Library, dated 1920. Only the series list, title page, and a motto from Thomas Traherne are present here. The motto marvels that an infant is heir of the whole world.Beyond the front matter, nothing is present to describe.
the-chums-of-scranton-high-or-hugh-morga: Donald Ferguson wrote this boys' school story, copyrighted in 1919 by the Goldsmith Publishing Company of Cleveland. Only the title page and contents are present here, with a frontispiece line in which Hugh speaks sternly. The chapters follow Hugh Morgan through a heavy task, a tragic affair on the road, a trap, a rescue at Hobson's Mill-Pond, and a straight drive for the truth.The chapters themselves remain out of view.
the-city-of-dreadful-night:
James Thomson's long poem opens under two dark mottoes, one from Dante and one from Leopardi. Dante's line points to the city of pain, and the Leopardi passage holds that fate denies blessedness to both the living and the dead. A proem in verse then explains why such a poem gets written at all.

The speaker writes, he says, prostrate in the dust, out of his heart's deep languor and his soul's sad tears. He asks why he should dig up dead faith and break the seals of mute despair. His answer is a cold rage that seizes him at times, driving him to show the bitter, wrinkled truth stripped of false dreams, false hopes, and the masks of youth. Fashioning woe into living words, however rough, gives some sense of power and passion. He writes not for the hopeful young, he warns, but for those who share his night.
the-fiend-s-delight:
Dod Grile, a pen name, gathered short comic tales in The Fiend's Delight, printed at New York in 1873. A mock preface and a sly dedication to the goddess Good Taste open the book.

The contents list dozens of brief sketches: One More Unfortunate, The Strong Young Man of Colusa, A Tale of the Great Quake, and Mr. Grile's Girl among them. West coast life, mining camps, and small town frauds feed the jokes. The tone is dry and cutting, in the school of tall tales told dead-pan, where fools, rogues, and bores each get a short, sharp lesson.
the-gibson-upright: Booth Tarkington and Harry Leon Wilson wrote The Gibson Upright as a play, printed in 1919. Only the front matter is present here. The cast list names Andrew Gibson, a piano factory owner. It names Nora Gorodna, a piano tester and socialist labor organizer. A socialist journalist stands in the list. A crew of factory workers, old and young, stands with them. Wives and a truck driver fill out the cast. A note says Stuart Walker staged the play. No scene or speech can be read here.
the-ignatian-epistles-entirely-spurious-:
W. D. Killen wrote this reply to Bishop Lightfoot of Durham. Killen taught church history in Ireland. He led the Presbyterian theological faculty there. Edinburgh saw the book in 1886. Lightfoot had argued for the letters of Ignatius. Seven letters are ascribed to that early martyr. Lightfoot called them genuine. He ranked them among the best proved writings of old times.

Killen's title gives the opposite verdict. The letters are wholly spurious, he argues. His preface protests against easy trust in a famous name. Such trust will sway a wide circle of readers. It would also upset the sound rules of history. He quotes Neander on the letters' weak stamp of a real man's voice. He praises Lightfoot's work on Scripture itself. The errors of a famed writer, he says, most need a challenge.
the-ladies-delight:
Printed for W. James in the Strand in 1732, this bawdy pamphlet cost sixpence. It gathers an address to all well provided Hibernians. A poem called The Arbor Vitae or Tree of Life follows. A prose natural history of the same tree comes next. A poem on Ridotto al' Fresco closes it. That poem describes the tree's growth in the Spring Gardens at Vauxhall. An ingenious botanist tends it there. The Latin motto warns that pleasure is a serious business.

The address opens the joke in a sustained plant metaphor. Irish gentlemen are congratulated on their gardens' largest trees. The ladies caress them for those trees, it says. Men of less parts are laughed at and shut out of company. The satire is a period piece of Grub-Street erotica. Innuendo about fruit, branches, and hopeful sticks fills it. A knowing coffee-house readership was its aim.
the-long-night: Stanley Weyman's The Long Night was issued by Longmans, Green, and Company in 1903, marked as a second impression. Only the title page, a list of Weyman's works, and part of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters open with A Student of Theology and The House on the Ramparts. Then come The Quintessential Stone, Caesar Basterga, The Elixir Vitae, and Melusina, pointing to a tale with alchemy in it. Weyman's listed works include A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe.
the-man-in-the-twilight: Ridgwell Cullum's The Man in the Twilight was published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1922. Only the title pages, a list of Cullum's novels, a dedication to his nephew, and an author's note are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. In that note Cullum stresses that his story of the Sachigo wood-pulp mills is a work of imagination. He drew heavily on his knowledge of the wood-pulp trade of Eastern Canada. The book contains no portrait of any person and no real business organisation.
the-northern-light:
E. Werner wrote the German novel The Northern Light, and Mrs. D. M. Lowrey translated it into English for this 1891 edition. Werner had earlier written At a High Price and His Word of Honor. The story opens on a grey autumn morning at a large manor house by a forest.

Two men watch birds fly south for the winter and talk about their own lives. One is a tall, blond officer named Falkenried, still young but already worn by care. His older companion tells him he takes life too hard. Their talk sets a somber mood of age, duty, and lost youth for the tale that follows.
the-princess-priscilla-s-fortnight:
Her Grand Ducal Highness the Princess Priscilla of Lothen-Kunitz was, up to twenty-one, a most promising young lady. She did what she was told, or better, sensed what was wanted and did it unasked. Her father, once fiery, is now an irritable old gentleman who insists on strict etiquette and is proud of her when she crosses his mind. Her English mother, original to the end, died when Priscilla was sixteen. Her two plainer sisters each married a suitable prince.

Priscilla herself is tall, with a long pointed chin and a sweet, kind mouth. Her nose is not quite straight, a slight crookedness the narrator finds charming beyond chiselled features. The book appeared in 1905 as by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden; an editorial note names that author as Elizabeth von Arnim. The narrator promises to describe Priscilla's dreadful conduct.
the-secret-of-the-night: Gaston Leroux's The Secret of the Night is dated 1912 in its header. The pages shown give a contents list of eighteen chapters and no story text. The first chapter is Gayety and Dynamite. Natacha, the watch, and a mysterious hand follow. Living bombs and marshes come later. A revolutionary tribunal and the last cravat close the list. A sibling record of this novel prints one chapter more, The Tsar.
the-street-called-straight:
Basil King published this novel in May 1912. He also wrote The Inner Shrine. Grosset and Dunlap issued it by arrangement with Harper and Brothers. Orson Lowell illustrated it. A New England motto heads the book. It speaks of coming by the street called Straight to the house called Beautiful. Chapter one finds Davenant back in the company of the hostess who once refused him.

Davenant is under no illusions about his welcome, King writes, but takes a mild pleasure in curiosity, admiration, and reminiscent suffering whose sting time has drawn. Between twenty-four and thirty-three, work and travel taught him much. A wider knowledge of men helped too. He now sees his proposal to Miss Guion as she saw it then. It was so ill-matched and absurd that it called for no reply. Not even a short no was needed.
the-tavern-knight: Rafael Sabatini's Tavern Knight, his 1904 novel, is represented here by a title and chapter list alone, with no page of the story itself. Eighteen chapters are named, opening on the march, passing through Worcester Field, and reaching the tavern knight's own story at chapter seven. Later headings promise an escape, the Ashburns, a metamorphosis of Kenneth, a reckoning, and a counter-plot. The skeleton points to an English Civil War adventure of loyalty and disguise, but Sabatini's swashbuckling prose remains outside this record.
thirty-years-in-hell-or-from-darkness-to: Ex-priest Bernard Fresenborg announced Thirty Years in Hell, or, From Darkness to Light, published at St. Louis and entered for copyright in 1904. Its title page says he spent thirty years in Roman Catholicism and now denounces it. The book runs to about four hundred large pages. Promotional lines call every page a stinging rebuke to Catholicism, and an author's announcement begins after the title matter. What is present here is the announcement's opening and the title pages, so Fresenborg's chapters themselves do not appear.
twelfth-night: Only production notes open this record, signed by Michael S. Hart of Project Gutenberg. The notes explain why the spelling in these old Shakespeare texts looks wrong to modern eyes. Printers, Hart says, packed type into blocks and swapped letters such as u and v when sorts ran short. He quotes three lines of Hamlet to show the old spellings kept unchanged here. No scene of the play itself is present in these pages.
waysiders-stories-of-connacht:
Seumas O'Kelly, author of The Shuiler's Child and The Lady of Deerpark, wrote Waysiders, stories of Connacht, issued at New York in 1918. The contents name ten tales. The Can with the Diamond Notch, Both Sides of the Pond, and The White Goat lead. The Sick Call, The Shoemaker, The Rector, and The Home-Coming follow. A Wayside Burial, The Gray Lake, and The Building close the list. The first tale opens on a shop sign in the west of Ireland.

The name stands out in chaste white letters on a black board. The shop itself seems to spring from the landscape with an air of aggression. It proclaims, he says, the clash of two civilisations, with the hills pitched against it. From such small fronts O'Kelly builds the inner life of Connacht villages, where old ways meet new money.
